topics.title: Meet Python: features and execution modes

learn.hook: Instagram, YouTube's tools, ISRO data analysis and NASA scripts all use Python. Your first line of it is just print('Hello').
points: A program is an ordered set of instructions for a computer; a programming language is the notation used to write it. Python is a high-level, interpreted, free and open-source language created by Guido van Rossum.

Features: simple, readable syntax; free and open source; interpreted (runs line by line); portable (same code runs on Windows, Linux, macOS); case-sensitive (Marks and marks differ); rich standard library; uses indentation to define blocks.
The Python interpreter (or the IDLE shell) shows the prompt >>>, where you can type a statement and see the result immediately.

Interactive mode: type one statement at >>> and get instant output; good for testing, but the code is not saved. Script mode: write the program in a file with the .py extension, save it, and run the whole file (in IDLE: Run → Run Module, or F5).

example.q: Write and run your first Python program in script mode.

learn.reallife: Python is used across Indian startups and research labs, from analysing monsoon data at IITM Pune to fintech apps in Bengaluru, because it is free, readable and has huge libraries.

learn.hook: Just as a sentence is made of words and punctuation, a Python statement is made of tokens. Some of those words are reserved, and you can't touch them.
points: Character set: the characters Python recognises: letters (A–Z, a–z), digits (0–9), special symbols (+ − * / ( ) [ ] { } : , ' " # etc.) and whitespace (space, tab, newline). Python 3 also accepts Unicode characters.
A token is the smallest meaningful unit of a program. Types: keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuators (delimiters).
Literals are fixed values written directly in code: 25, 3.14, 'Delhi', True, None. Operators perform operations: +, ==, and. Punctuators structure the code: ( ) [ ] { } , : etc.
Keywords are reserved words with a special meaning, e.g. if, else, elif, for, while, True, False, None, and, or, not, def, import, in, is. They cannot be used as identifiers.
Keywords are case-sensitive: True is a keyword but true is not. print and input are built-in function names, not keywords.

example.answer: Keyword, identifiers, operator, literals and punctuators

learn.reallife: A railway announcement system's code might say: if delay > 30: announce(...). Here if is a keyword, delay an identifier, 30 a literal and > an operator.

learn.hook: Naming a variable x1 works. Naming it total_marks works better. Naming it 1st_rank crashes your code.
points: An identifier is a name given to a variable, function or other object.

Rules: it can contain letters (A–Z, a–z), digits (0–9) and underscore (_); it must start with a letter or underscore, not a digit; no spaces or special symbols like @, $, %, -, .; it cannot be a keyword; it is case-sensitive.
Good practice: use meaningful names (total_marks, not t), separate words with underscores. An identifier can be of any length.
A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line. The interpreter ignores it; it explains code to humans.
A docstring is a string in triple quotes ("""...""") placed as the first statement of a module or function to document it.

learn.hook: In Python, a variable is not a box that holds a value. It's a name tag tied to an object in memory, and you can move the tag.
points: A variable is a name that refers to a value (object) stored in memory. Python needs no explicit declaration; a variable is created when it is first assigned.
Assignment uses =: the right side (r-value, an expression) is evaluated first, then the name on the left (l-value) is made to refer to it. 5 = x is an error because 5 cannot be an l-value.
Multiple assignment: a = b = c = 0 gives all three the value 0; x, y, z = 1, 2, 3 assigns each in turn. x, y = y, x swaps two values.
Everything in Python is an object with an identity (its location in memory), a type and a value. id(x) returns the identity; type(x) returns the type.

topics.title: Data types: numbers, sequences, sets, None and dictionaries

learn.hook: Is 9876543210 a number or a string? For a phone number, you'll want a string. Picking the right type is half of programming.
points: Numbers: int (whole numbers like −5, 2026), float (with a decimal point, like 3.14, 2.0) and complex (like 3 + 4j). bool (True/False) is a subtype of int, so True + True = 2.
Sequences (ordered collections): str (characters in quotes, 'India'), list (in square brackets, mutable, [1, 'a', 2.5]) and tuple (in parentheses, immutable, (10, 20)).
Set: an unordered collection of unique items in braces, e.g. {1, 2, 3}; duplicates are removed automatically.
None: a special value meaning absence of a value; its type is NoneType.
Mapping: a dictionary (dict) stores key : value pairs in braces, e.g. {'roll': 12, 'name': 'Asha'}.

example.answer: int, float, str, list, tuple, set, dict, bool, NoneType, complex

learn.reallife: A UPI transaction record might use a str for the UPI ID, a float for the amount, a bool for success and a dict to bundle them together.

topics.title: Mutable vs immutable, and choosing a data type

learn.hook: You can change a list in place but not a string. Try s[0] = 'J' on 'Python' and Python refuses. Why?
points: Mutable types can be changed in place after creation: list, dictionary, set. Their id() stays the same when you modify their contents.
Immutable types cannot be changed in place: int, float, bool, complex, str, tuple. 'Changing' them actually creates a new object; the variable then refers to the new object (a different id).
Example: x = 10; x = x + 1 makes x refer to a NEW object 11. L = [1, 2]; L.append(3) changes the SAME list.

Choosing types: use a list for a collection that will change (shopping cart), a tuple for fixed data (days of the week, coordinates), a dictionary for fast lookup by key (roll number → name), a set for unique items, and type() to check a value's type.

example.q: Predict: L = [1, 2]; before = id(L); L.append(3); is id(L) == before? And for s = 'ab'; before = id(s); s = s + 'c'?
steps: append changes the same list object in place → ids are equal → True
s + 'c' creates a new string 'abc'; s now refers to it → ids differ → False
example.answer: List: True (same object). String: False (new object).

learn.reallife: An e-commerce cart (items added/removed) should be a list or dict, while the fixed list of Indian states and UTs in a form can safely be a tuple.

learn.hook: 7 / 2 is 3.5, 7 // 2 is 3, and −7 // 2 is −4, not −3. Python's operators have a few surprises worth knowing.
points: Arithmetic: + − * (multiply), / (true division, always a float), // (floor division: rounds DOWN to the nearest whole number), % (remainder/modulus), ** (exponent).

Augmented assignment: x += 3 means x = x + 3. Similarly −=, *=, /=, %=, //=, **=.

learn.hook: 0 or 'Guest' gives 'Guest'. In Python, and/or don't always return True or False; they return one of the operands!
points: Logical operators: and (True only if both are True), or (True if at least one is True), not (reverses). They short-circuit: evaluation stops as soon as the result is known.
Truth values: 0, 0.0, '' (empty string), [], (), {}, None and False are falsy; everything else is truthy.
With non-Boolean operands: x and y returns x if x is falsy, else y. x or y returns x if x is truthy, else y. not always returns True or False. e.g. 0 or 5 → 5; 3 and 0 → 0; 5 and 7 → 7.
Identity operators: is and is not check whether two names refer to the SAME object (same id), not just equal values.
Membership operators: in and not in test whether a value is present in a sequence (string, list, tuple) or is a key of a dictionary.

learn.hook: 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512, not 64. Knowing which operator goes first is the difference between full marks and zero.
points: An expression is a combination of values, variables and operators that Python evaluates to a single value: 3 + 4 * 2, x > 5, 'a' * 3.
Precedence (highest first): ( ) parentheses → ** → unary −, + → * / // % → binary + − → relational (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) → not → and → or.
Associativity: operators of equal precedence are evaluated left to right, EXCEPT ** which is right to left: 2 ** 3 ** 2 = 2 ** 9 = 512.
Since ** binds tighter than unary minus, −2 ** 2 = −(2 ** 2) = −4. Use parentheses (−2) ** 2 = 4 when you mean it.
A statement is a unit of code that Python executes, e.g. x = 5, print(x), if ...: An expression produces a value; a statement performs an action (an expression can be part of a statement).

topics.title: Debugging: syntax, logical and runtime errors

learn.hook: The program runs, no red text, but your average of 80 and 90 comes out as 125. That's the sneakiest kind of bug.
points: Debugging is the process of finding and removing errors (bugs) from a program.
Syntax error: the code breaks the rules of the language (missing colon, unmatched bracket, misspelt keyword). Python refuses to run the program. e.g. print('Hi' → SyntaxError.

Logical error: the program runs without crashing but gives the wrong output because the logic is wrong, e.g. average = a + b / 2 instead of (a + b) / 2. Python gives no message, so these are hardest to find.

Runtime error (exception): the program starts but stops during execution, e.g. ZeroDivisionError (10 / 0), ValueError (int('abc')), TypeError ('5' + 2), NameError (using an undefined name), IndexError.
Exam tasks: identify valid identifiers, evaluate expressions, predict output, name the error type, and write small programs.

example.q: Classify: (a) if x > 5 print(x)  (b) avg = a + b / 2  (c) print(10 / n) with n = 0

(c) Starts running, then crashes when dividing by zero → runtime error (ZeroDivisionError)

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu's average program gives 125 for 80 and 90 without any error message. Explain the three types of errors and debugging.
teach.praise: So it's a logical error — the code runs but the formula is wrong. Syntax errors stop it from starting and runtime errors crash it midway!
teach.nudge: Good. Can you name the three error types and say which one runs but gives wrong output?

revise.summary: Debugging is finding and fixing errors. Syntax errors break the language rules and stop the program from running; logical errors give wrong output without any message; runtime errors (exceptions) like ZeroDivisionError, ValueError, TypeError, NameError and IndexError stop a running program.
focus: Classify errors as syntax, logical or runtime
Name common runtime exceptions
Explain why logical errors are hardest to find
remember: Syntax error: rules broken (missing colon, unmatched bracket); the program does not run
Logical error: runs but gives wrong output (avg = a + b / 2)
Runtime errors: ZeroDivisionError, ValueError, TypeError, NameError, IndexError
traps: IndentationError is a syntax error, not a runtime error
Logical errors do not break syntax rules
